The articles and help pages use the terms below in these senses.

The terms, A to Z: [area of applicability (AOA)](#area-of-applicability),
[autocorrelation range](#autocorrelation-range), [backend](#backend),
[block](#block), [cell](#cell), [cell's true mean](#cells-true-mean), [CRS
units](#crs-units), [design effect (`deff`)](#design-effect), [dissimilarity
index (DI)](#dissimilarity-index), [flat region](#flat-region),
[fold](#fold), [level](#level), [lon/lat](#lon-lat), [nugget, sill,
range](#nugget-sill-range), [pooled value](#pooled-value), [range
floor](#range-floor), [row ID](#row-id), [size](#size), [support
ceiling](#support-ceiling), [variogram](#variogram).

[area of applicability (AOA)]{#area-of-applicability}
:   The prediction locations where a model's cross-validated score can be
    expected to hold: those whose dissimilarity index is at or below a
    threshold, the largest dissimilarity index of the training rows that is
    not an outlier. `area_of_applicability()` computes it.

[autocorrelation range]{#autocorrelation-range}
:   The distance beyond which two observations are close to uncorrelated, in
    the units of the CRS the variogram is fitted in. `estimate_sac_range()`
    returns it as the effective range of an exponential variogram: three
    times the fitted range parameter, where the semivariance has covered
    about 95 percent of the rise from the nugget to the sill. A block or a buffer has to exceed it to keep
    held-out rows apart from their training data.

[backend]{#backend}
:   One of the three model fitters behind the `spatial_fit` class: the
    random forest (`fit_rf_model()`), GWR (geographically weighted
    regression, `fit_gwr_model()`) and the Bayesian GP (a Bayesian model
    with a Gaussian-process term in the coordinates,
    `fit_bayesian_spatial_model()`). `new_spatial_fit()` wraps a model of
    your own in the same class.

[block]{#block}
:   A piece of the study area that a fold holds out whole: a cell of a
    rectangular grid, at least `block_size` on each side when that is given,
    or one of the polygons passed in `blocks`.
    `make_folds(method = "block_kfold")` builds the grid.

[cell]{#cell}
:   A polygon of a tessellation: a Voronoi cell, a hexagon, a square or a
    Delaunay triangle. `assign_features_to_polygons()` puts each observation
    in one cell, and the `poly_id` column names it.

[cell's true mean]{#cells-true-mean}
:   What a cell value estimates: the expected value of one further
    observation located in the cell the way its observations were. It is not
    the average of a surface over the cell's area, which would give weight to
    ground that holds no observation. "Pooled values" in
    `?summarize_by_cell` defines it.

[CRS units]{#crs-units}
:   The unit of the coordinate reference system a function works in, such
    as the metre for a UTM zone. Distances, block sizes, bandwidths and
    ranges are given in it. A function that measures distances moves a
    lon/lat layer into a projected CRS that `ensure_projected()` chooses,
    whose unit is the metre (`?"spatialkit-geometry"`).

[design effect (`deff`)]{#design-effect}
:   The factor by which correlation among a cell's observations inflates the
    variance of the cell mean as an estimate of the population mean;
    `n / deff` is then the cell's effective sample size.
    `summarize_by_cell(deff = )` applies it to the standard errors. At the
    default, `deff = 1`, the standard error is that of the cell's own mean,
    which needs no such correction when the cell's observations are spread
    through it.

[dissimilarity index (DI)]{#dissimilarity-index}
:   The distance from a prediction location to the nearest training row in
    the space of the predictors, each centred and scaled by the training
    data's own mean and standard deviation and weighted by importance when
    the model carries it, divided by the mean distance between training
    rows. Meyer and Pebesma (2021) define it, and `area_of_applicability()`
    computes it.

[flat region]{#flat-region}
:   The levels whose criterion value is within `tol` of the optimum, which
    `select_resolution()` returns with the count it chooses. The criteria
    do not rise or fall steadily with the count, so the flat region is a set
    of levels that can leave out some in between. Report it with the count.

[fold]{#fold}
:   One split of a cross-validation: the rows held out and the rows the
    model is trained on to predict them. `make_folds()` returns the folds,
    each a `train` and a `test` set of row IDs.

[level]{#level}
:   A candidate cell count on the ladder that `resolution_profile()` scores.
    `select_resolution()` chooses one of the levels.

[lon/lat]{#lon-lat}
:   Coordinates in degrees of longitude and latitude, in a geographic CRS.
    See [CRS units](#crs-units) for how distances are measured on such a
    layer.

[nugget, sill, range]{#nugget-sill-range}
:   The variogram's value at zero distance (the noise), the value it levels
    off at (the total variance), and the range, the distance over which it
    rises toward the sill. The exponential model `estimate_sac_range()` fits
    approaches the sill without reaching it; see
    [autocorrelation range](#autocorrelation-range). `sac_nugget()` reads the nugget of an `estimate_sac_range()` result.

[pooled value]{#pooled-value}
:   A cell's mean pulled toward the mean of the observations in the 8
    nearest cells (nearest by the centroid of their observations). The own
    weight, the share of the pooled value that is the cell's own mean, grows
    with the cell's count. `summarize_by_cell()` returns pooled values
    beside the plain means by default (`estimate = "pooled"`), and "Pooled
    values" in its help gives the formula.

[range floor]{#range-floor}
:   The fewest cells the autocorrelation range allows: the area of the
    points' convex hull divided by the square of the range, rounded up, and
    at least 2. A cell wider than the range averages over more than one
    patch of the field. `resolution_profile()` reports the floor and by
    default does not apply it;
    `select_resolution(criterion = "reliability")` reads the levels from the
    floor up.

[row ID]{#row-id}
:   `..row_id`, the column by which folds, cross-validated predictions and
    the record of dropped rows name rows. The `cv_*()` functions number the
    rows in it when a layer has none. `make_folds()` names rows by this
    column when the layer has it, and by row position otherwise.

[size]{#size}
:   The mean number of observations a cell is to hold, `obs_per_cell` in
    `resolution_profile()`. A size `s` gives `max(2, round(n / s))` cells,
    with `n` the rows that carry a response, or every point without one. The
    default profile scores one size, 4.5, and that sets the default count of
    cells for pooled values.

[support ceiling]{#support-ceiling}
:   The most cells the data support on a ladder of counts: the scored rows
    (those with a response and every predictor, or every point without a
    response) divided by `min_cell_n`, 9 by default, rounded down. On a
    ladder of sizes the finest level takes its place. When a criterion's
    optimum sits on the ceiling or on the range floor, that bound sets the
    count, and `select_resolution()` names it in `edge`.

[variogram]{#variogram}
:   The semivariance of a variable against the distance between pairs of
    points, where the semivariance is half the mean squared difference of
    the pairs at that distance. `estimate_sac_range()` fits an exponential
    model with a nugget to it, and `plot()` on the result
    (`?plot.sac_range`) draws the variogram, with the fitted model where a
    range was identified.

## Next

This is the last article in reading order. The help pages that give these
terms in full are `?area_of_applicability`, `?estimate_sac_range`,
`?make_folds`, `?resolution_profile`, `?select_resolution`,
`?summarize_by_cell` and `?"spatialkit-geometry"`. `?spatialkit` lists every
step of the pipeline with its functions.

## References

Meyer, H. and Pebesma, E. (2021). Predicting into unknown space? Estimating
the area of applicability of spatial prediction models. *Methods in Ecology
and Evolution* 12(9), 1620–1633.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13650>
